evidence: Read src/sqllens/memory/io.py at head. parse_json (134-156) calls json.loads; `except RecursionError` (140-145) raises BundleFormatError(_TOO_DEEP_MESSAGE). On success it runs _enforce_depth_cap (98-113, iterative, raises BundleFormatError(_TOO_DEEP_MESSAGE) when depth > MAX_BUNDLE_DEPTH=64) before the root-type check. So both outcomes for deep input (value returned, or RecursionError) give the same 'bundle JSON is too deeply nested to parse safely' message; the comment at 30-33 states this. Per CPython, the C scanner (Modules/_json.c scan_once_unicode) guards each container with Py_EnterRecursiveCall, bounded by the recursion limit (default 1000 in 3.11, a limit on the order of hundreds to thousands of nested levels). 65 nested levels plus ordinary caller frames (even under pytest) is far under 1000, so json.loads returns and the payload reaches _enforce_depth_cap. I did not execute Python (no shell tool), so this rests on reading the source and knowledge of CPython recursion handling.

io.py:30-34 comment says json.loads on 3.11 raises RecursionError under 1,000 levels. In CPython 3.11 Modules/_json.c scan_once_unicode calls Py_EnterRecursiveCall for each '[' / '{' level, and in 3.11 that counter is the same one as the Python recursion limit (default 1000, reduced by the caller's existing frame depth). So '['*999+'1'+']'*999 called from any non-trivial stack exceeds the budget and raises RecursionError, i.e. below 1,000 levels. 3.12+ separates the C recursion limit, which explains the old base 'several thousand' claim and the 3.11 contrast. The input is for the default recursion limit, which the comment implies. I could not run Python 3.11 here (no execution tool), so this rests on CPython source knowledge. Side note: the RecursionError handler (io.py:140-145) maps to the same _TOO_DEEP_MESSAGE as the depth cap, so the 'message differs by Python version' rationale is loose, but that is not the claim checked.

io.py:98-113: _enforce_depth_cap uses a while-loop over an explicit stack with no self-call (only BundleFormatError raise and isinstance/pop/append calls), so it is iterative. Both stack.append calls (lines 105, 113) are guarded by isinstance(..., (dict, list)). Trace: scalar root '1' -> line 104 false, stack empty, loop skipped. Dict with scalar values -> root pushed, popped, children iterated, no scalar pushed. Hostile input: deeply nested list cannot cause recursion; only containers are pushed.

io.py:103-113: root dict/list is pushed at depth 1, each nested dict/list child is pushed at depth+1, and the check `depth > MAX_BUNDLE_DEPTH` (=64, io.py:34) runs on pop, so it raises only at depth 65 or more. A scalar root is never pushed, so the loop does nothing and passes. Builders (test_memory_schema_io.py:136-145): _nested_arrays(n) has n array levels, so the innermost is at depth n (64 passes, 65 raises). _object_over_arrays(n) is one object plus n-1 arrays, so max depth is n. _nested_objects(n) has n objects, so max depth is n. The hint's '{"x": ' + '['*63 ... + '}' payload has max depth 1+63 = 64 and passes; the 65 variant has 65 and fails. Absolute-claim input traced: a wide, mixed object/array payload is covered because every container is stack-walked with its own depth and none is skipped.

io.py:136-148: json.loads sits in a try; the `except RecursionError` branch (140-145) raises BundleFormatError(_TOO_DEEP_MESSAGE), so control leaves parse_json before _enforce_depth_cap at line 148; a RecursionError cannot reach the walk. RecursionError subclasses RuntimeError, not json.JSONDecodeError (a ValueError subclass), so the line-138 handler would not catch it. Callers: cli.py:457-461 catches only BundleFormatError around parse_json, so an uncaught RecursionError would escape. server.py:424-427 catches only BundleFormatError around parse_json; the broad `except Exception` at 440 covers only import_bundle, not parse_json. Absolute-claim input traced: a deeply nested array/object text (e.g. '['*100000) passed to server import_memory or cli import_memory; without the handler it would bypass both except BundleFormatError clauses. Claim holds.

tests/unit/test_memory_schema_io.py:149-150 comments that on Python 3.14 json.loads parses _nested_arrays(10_000) without RecursionError. issue-context.md line 21 records the observed behavior on 3.14.7: json.loads parses 100,000 levels and raises RecursionError only beyond that (about 116,000 on a macOS main thread). Line 16 and 21 also show the failing test got 'bundle root must be a JSON object' on 3.14, which is what happens only when json.loads succeeds. 10,000 levels is well under 100,000, so the comment is accurate. Absolute-claim input: the 10,000-level array payload (the test's own input). The 100,000-level observation covers it. Caveat: the threshold depends on thread stack size (about 116,000 on a macOS main thread), and I did not run CPython 3.14 or read Modules/_json.c. The PASS rests on the issue's recorded reproduction.

At depth 64, _enforce_depth_cap (io.py:98-113) only raises when depth > MAX_BUNDLE_DEPTH, so it passes. Arrays shape: root is a list, so parse_json raises 'bundle root must be a JSON object' (io.py:149-150). Object shapes {"x": [...]} and {"a": {...}}: root is a dict, so MemoryBundle.model_validate runs; MemoryBundle has model_config extra='forbid' (schema.py:100), so unknown keys 'x'/'a' raise ValidationError, mapped to BundleFormatError via _fmt_err (io.py:151-154), which joins validation lines and does not include the depth message. Nesting counts: _object_over_arrays(64) = 1 object + 63 arrays = 64; _nested_objects(64) = 64. json.loads handles depth 64 without RecursionError. The claim's assumption holds.

load_golden (src/sqllens/eval/golden.py:51) calls parse_json(text) for json with no except/rewrap. parse_json (src/sqllens/memory/io.py:134-148) maps RecursionError from json.loads to BundleFormatError(_TOO_DEEP_MESSAGE) (line 140-145), and otherwise runs the iterative _enforce_depth_cap (MAX_BUNDLE_DEPTH=64), which raises the same message for a parsed structure deeper than 64 (lines 98-113); this runs before the root-type check.
